metadata.title: Seeded Faults — Final Project Pitch
metadata.topic: Pitch for a Claude Code workflow that scores AI-written data-quality tests against planted faults
metadata.purpose: INFO 7375 final project pitch film. Pitch, not a build: nothing in the project exists yet.
metadata.author: Atharva C
metadata.voice_kokoro: TBD — pick a Kokoro voice that is not an instructor persona voice (not am_onyx / af_bella); record choice in FRICTIONAL.md
metadata.format_note: show-tell style: one simple drawn picture per beat, minimal on-screen text, narration carries the idea. Any mock-up beat carries an on-screen 'CONSTRUCTED' label.

beats.narration_text: I'm Atharva, and I want to be hired as a data engineer. My final project will be called Seeded Faults: a Claude Code workflow that writes data-quality tests for a table, and then checks whether those tests actually catch problems.
beats.new_visual_element: A single table icon with a row of checkmarks beside it, one checkmark drawn with a question mark

beats.narration_text: When it's done, it will be a public GitHub repository: a fault-injection script, a small dbt project on DuckDB, the prompt contract Claude follows, an evaluation log, and a write-up of what the tests missed. None of that exists yet. Today there's this plan and one small test I ran by hand.
beats.new_visual_element: Repository folder tree drawn as boxes; each box stamped 'WILL EXIST'

beats.narration_text: Here's the problem. When you add tests to a new table, they pass on clean data, and that feels like safety. But a test that has never failed hasn't proven anything. My guess is that AI-written tests make this worse, because they look complete. That's what I want to measure.
beats.new_visual_element: Green 'all tests passed' badge, with a crack running through it

beats.narration_text: I looked at tools data engineers already use. In Great Expectations, version 1.24, I wrote each check by hand. When I planted fifty missing values, my check caught all fifty. dbt gave the same result with tests I wrote in YAML, and the dbt-expectations package adds more test types, but you still write them yourself. In each case, a test only checks what you thought to write. None of them told me what my tests would miss. That score is what Seeded Faults will add.
beats.new_visual_element: Three tool boxes (Great Expectations, dbt, dbt-expectations), each with a hand-written checklist; a fourth box with a caught/missed scoreboard
beats.evidence: Ran 2026-10-09 in sandbox: GX 1.24.0 and dbt 1.12.5 not_null check — clean sample 0 failures, 50 planted nulls → 50 caught. dbt-expectations README read 2026-10-09 (hub.getdbt.com/metaplane/dbt_expectations, v0.10.10). See FRICTIONAL.md.

beats.narration_text: The reader is a data engineering hiring manager. In the first sixty seconds, they open the README and see one table: every planted fault, caught or missed, and why. One command reproduces it.
beats.new_visual_element: Mock README with a caught/missed table — rows blank or clearly placeholder

beats.narration_text: It will show the skills this course teaches: a written prompt contract, verification instead of trust, and an evaluation you can rerun. And it will show data engineering: SQL, dbt, and thinking about keys and grain. The evidence will be the log in the repo, not a claim in this film.
beats.new_visual_element: Three linked icons: contract, magnifier, repeat-loop; arrow to a log file

beats.narration_text: In scope: one public table of New York City taxi trips, a fixed catalogue of about fifteen to twenty fault types, and the generated tests. Out of scope: it will not repair data or touch a live warehouse. The first thing I'll build is a fault-injection script that covers the whole catalogue. You'll know it ran when the eval command prints a caught-or-missed table.
beats.new_visual_element: A box split IN / OUT; a '1' badge on the fault-injection script

beats.narration_text: What could sink it: Claude might write tests that pass everything and catch little, or tests so strict they flag clean data. So I'll measure false alarms on clean data as well as catches, and I'll fix the fault list before generating any tests, so I can't tune one to the other.
beats.new_visual_element: A balance: 'missed faults' on one side, 'false alarms' on the other

beats.narration_text: Why this project? It's a mix. I already work with SQL and data pipelines. You can open my Crime Rate Management System on GitHub: an Oracle database I built on my own, with its own testing script. What's new for me is prompt contracts, evaluating an AI's output, and fault injection.
beats.new_visual_element: Two columns: 'already have' (with a drawn repo card labelled DMDD_FinalProject) and 'learning'
beats.evidence: Public repos checked 2026-10-09 via GitHub API: github.com/Arc-211/DMDD_FinalProject (CRMS, solo; SQL + testing.sql) and github.com/Arc-211/Chinook_ADF (ADF pipeline JSON). LA crime project is not public, so not cited.

beats.narration_text: So that's Seeded Faults: tests for your data, tested. The project isn't built yet. The first step is the fault-injection script, and the log of how it goes will be in the repository.
beats.new_visual_element: The cracked badge from B02, now beside a scoreboard with empty rows
